title: Maple Ridge Dental Supply: analyzing the accounts payable process and defining system requirements
participant_role: Staff accountant assigned to an accounts payable process improvement project
judge_role: Controller of Maple Ridge Dental Supply, who is considering an automated accounts payable system

difficulty.rationale: Process metrics, savings and system requirements.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a staff accountant at MAPLE RIDGE DENTAL SUPPLY, a distributor of dental equipment and supplies. The controller (judge) has assigned you to a process improvement project on the accounts payable (AP) process.

MAPLE RIDGE DENTAL SUPPLY processes about 1,200 vendor invoices a month, and the controller (judge) is frustrated. Vendors call about late payments, the company pays late fees, and the AP clerk is always behind. The controller (judge) is considering buying an automated AP system but first wants to understand what is really wrong with the current process, what it costs, and what a new system would need to do before talking with software vendors.

You observed the AP clerk for a week, reviewed twelve months of AP records and gathered industry benchmark data. Your findings are summarized below.

[Current AP process: see exhibits]

[AP costs, discounts and benchmark: see exhibits]

The controller (judge) wants a clear picture of the problem supported by numbers, and a list of requirements that can be given to software vendors.

You must:
- Explain how business analysis connects to business process management
- Identify the core problem in the accounts payable process
- Analyze the current process using efficiency measures and the benchmark
- Define the business, functional and nonfunctional requirements for an automated accounts payable system
- Define the data needed for the new system and its limitations

You will present the information to the controller (judge) in a role-play to take place in the controller's office. The controller (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the controller's (judge's) questions, the controller (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Won't automation eliminate internal controls if no one looks at invoices?
How will we know the new system worked a year from now?

solution.overview: A strong answer shows that slow manual matching and email approvals create a 12 day cycle that misses most early payment discounts. Clerk time of 23 minutes per invoice costs $11.50 per invoice, or $13,800 a month, versus $3,600 at the $3 benchmark (a $10,200 monthly saving). Missed discounts of $15,200 a month plus $1,800 of late fees bring the total opportunity to about $27,200 a month. The presenter lists business, functional and nonfunctional requirements for an automated system and identifies the data needed and its limitations.

by_task.task: Business analysis and business process management
answer: Business process management (BPM) designs, measures and improves how work flows through the company
Business analysis studies a process, finds problems and defines what a solution must do
Business analysis supplies the facts and requirements that BPM uses to redesign the process
Together they make sure a new system fixes the real problem instead of automating a bad process
Manual matching and email approvals create a 12 day cycle from receipt to payment
Discounts require payment within 10 days, so most discounts are missed
Checks printed only once a week add more delay
Manual keying causes errors (3% of invoices, about 36 a month) such as duplicates
Clerk time: 5 + 12 + 6 = 23 minutes per invoice, costing 23 / 60 x $30 = $11.50 per invoice
Monthly cost: 1,200 x $11.50 = $13,800 versus 1,200 x $3 = $3,600 at the benchmark, saving $10,200
Missed discounts: 380 invoices x $40 = $15,200 a month
Total opportunity: 10,200 + 15,200 + 1,800 late fees = about $27,200 a month
Cycle time 12 days versus the 3 day benchmark

by_task.task: Requirements for an automated AP system
answer: Business: pay within discount windows, cut cost per invoice to about $3, eliminate late fees
Functional: capture invoices electronically with OCR, automatic three way match, approval workflow with reminders
Functional: duplicate invoice detection and ACH electronic payments
Nonfunctional: security and user access controls, audit trail, integration with the accounting system
Nonfunctional: reliable uptime and ease of use for the clerk and approvers
Vendor master file (names, addresses, payment terms, bank information)
Purchase order and receiving report data for the three way match
Invoice fields: vendor, invoice number, date, terms and amount
Limitations: inconsistent vendor names, paper invoices, missing receiving reports and only 12 months of history

calculations.label: Missed purchase discounts
steps: Invoices offering a discount: 480; discounts taken: 100

calculations.label: Total monthly opportunity
steps: Processing savings $10,200 + missed discounts $15,200 + late fees $1,800 = $27,200

judge_question_answers.question: Won't automation eliminate internal controls if no one looks at invoices?
answer: No: a well designed system strengthens controls instead of removing them
The automatic three way match checks every invoice against the purchase order and receiving report
Invoices that do not match or exceed limits are sent to a person for review
Approval workflows, user access controls and an audit trail show who approved what and when

judge_question_answers.question: How will we know the new system worked a year from now?
answer: Measure the same key performance indicators before and after the change
Cost per invoice (goal about $3) and cycle time (goal about 3 days)
Discount capture rate (goal close to all 480 eligible invoices) and late fees (goal zero)
Error rate (duplicates and wrong amounts) below today's 3%

key_concepts.definition: A method for designing, measuring and continuously improving how work flows through an organization.
Studying a business need or problem and defining the requirements for a solution.
The time from the start to the end of a process; here, from receiving an invoice to paying it.
A standard or best practice measure used to compare performance, such as $3 per invoice for automated AP.
Comparing the purchase order, receiving report and vendor invoice before paying, to make sure the company pays only for what it ordered and received.
A 2% discount if the invoice is paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days.
High level goals the solution must achieve, such as paying within discount windows.
What the system must do, such as capture invoices, match documents and route approvals.
How well the system must perform, such as security, reliability, speed and ease of use.
A record showing who entered, changed or approved each transaction and when.
A measure used to track progress toward a goal, such as cost per invoice or discount capture rate.

notes: State level because students must turn process observations into cost, discount and benchmark figures and then classify requirements correctly. Watch for students who count all 480 invoices as missed discounts instead of 380, who forget the late fees, or who mix up functional and nonfunctional requirements.

items.label: Discuss the connection between business analysis and business process management

criteria.exceeds: Explains that business process management designs, measures and improves how work flows, that business analysis finds the problems and defines what a solution must do, and that together they make sure the new AP system fixes the real problem instead of automating a bad process.
criteria.meets: Explains that business analysis supplies the facts and requirements that business process management uses to redesign the AP process.
criteria.below: Defines one of the two terms but does not explain how they connect.
criteria.little: Does not discuss business analysis or business process management.

criteria.exceeds: Classifies requirements correctly and specifically: business (pay within discount windows, cost of about $3 per invoice, no late fees), functional (electronic capture with OCR, automatic three way match, approval workflow with reminders, duplicate detection, ACH payments) and nonfunctional (security and access controls, audit trail, integration, uptime, ease of use).
criteria.meets: Lists business, functional and nonfunctional requirements for the automated AP system with at least one correct example of each.
criteria.below: Lists features for the system but does not separate them into types, or mixes up functional and nonfunctional requirements.
criteria.little: Does not define requirements, or lists items unrelated to the AP problem.

criteria.exceeds: Identifies the core problem as slow manual matching and email approvals (4 day wait) creating a 12 day cycle when discounts require payment within 10 days, made worse by weekly check runs and manual keying errors on 3% of invoices (about 36 a month).
criteria.meets: Identifies that the manual process creates a 12 day cycle time, so most 10 day discounts are missed and late fees are paid.
criteria.below: Names symptoms (late fees, a busy clerk) without identifying the cause in the process.
criteria.little: Does not identify a process problem, or blames the clerk alone.

criteria.exceeds: Defines the data needed (vendor master file with names, addresses, terms and bank information; purchase order and receiving report data for the three way match; invoice fields such as vendor, number, date, terms and amount) and the limitations: inconsistent vendor names, paper invoices, missing receiving reports and only 12 months of history.
criteria.meets: Names the vendor master file, purchase order and receiving report data, and invoice fields as data needs, and identifies at least two limitations.
criteria.below: Lists some data needs but gives no limitations, or the limitations are vague.
criteria.little: Does not define data needs or limitations.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates 23 clerk minutes per invoice at $11.50 each ($13,800 a month) versus $3,600 at the $3 benchmark (saving $10,200), missed discounts of 380 x $40 = $15,200, and a total opportunity of about $27,200 a month with the $1,800 of late fees, and compares the 12 day cycle with the 3 day benchmark.
criteria.meets: Calculates the $11.50 cost per invoice, the $10,200 monthly saving versus the benchmark and the $15,200 of missed discounts, and compares cycle time with the benchmark.
criteria.below: Gets only part of the analysis, for example counts all 480 invoices as missed discounts or leaves out the late fees.
criteria.little: Does not analyze the process with numbers, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibits.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects each process step to cycle time, missed discounts, late fees and cost, and shows how the requirements target each cause.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the process observations to the core problem and the $27,200 monthly opportunity.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how delays cause missed discounts.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the controller a clear recommendation to pursue automation backed by the $27,200 monthly opportunity, with a ready list of requirements to give software vendors.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation and provides requirements the controller can use with software vendors.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.

criteria.exceeds: Presents the problem, numbers and requirements in plain language and a logical order the controller could share with software vendors, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the problem, analysis, requirements and data needs clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual such as a process flow of the five steps or a current versus benchmark table, and adds a useful idea such as moving vendors to electronic invoices.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the problem and the savings easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: automation strengthens controls through the automatic three way match, sending exceptions to a person, approval workflows, access controls and an audit trail; and success is measured by KPIs against today's baseline (cost per invoice near $3, cycle time near 3 days, discounts captured on nearly all 480 eligible invoices, zero late fees, errors below 3%).
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that exceptions still go to a person and that success is measured by comparing cost, cycle time and discounts before and after.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees that automation removes internal controls.

key_points: Core problem: manual matching and email approvals create a 12 day cycle, so most discounts requiring payment within 10 days are missed
Clerk time 5 + 12 + 6 = 23 minutes per invoice at $30 an hour = $11.50 per invoice, or $13,800 a month
Benchmark cost 1,200 x $3 = $3,600 a month, a saving of $10,200 a month; benchmark cycle time is 3 days
Missed discounts: (480 minus 100) = 380 invoices x $40 = $15,200 a month
Total opportunity: $10,200 + $15,200 + $1,800 late fees = about $27,200 a month

Requirements: business (discounts, about $3 per invoice, no late fees), functional (OCR capture, three way match, approval workflow, duplicate detection, ACH), nonfunctional (security, audit trail, integration, uptime, ease of use)

Data needs: vendor master file, purchase order and receiving data, invoice fields; limitations include inconsistent vendor names, paper invoices, missing receiving reports and only 12 months of history
